The biggest wage negotiation of Chile’s mining year has begun at Escondida, the world’s biggest copper mine. The supervisors’ union filed its demands in mid-August and asked BHP for what it calls a fair sharing of the wealth.

Because copper is near record prices and BHP has just posted bumper profits, the workers think their timing is good.

Who Is Actually At The Table

The union that opened talks is Sindicato N°2 de Supervisores de Minera Escondida. It has 1,020 active members, although it was only founded in 2014.

That matters, because the older operators’ and maintainers’ union, Sindicato N°1, has richer benefits built up over decades. The supervisors say they simply want to level the playing field.

The Demand, In The Union’s Own Words

Union president Alexis Barrera told Diario Financiero that high prices, record output and historic company results all point one way. So the union is pushing for more.

His phrase was blunt: the union wants a “fair sharing of the wealth with the workers”. Still, he framed it as a chance to settle without a fight.

The Clock On The Escondida Contract

The union handed over its proposal in mid-August, and BHP’s formal reply was due within days. The current collective contract expires on September 30, 2026.

That date is the real deadline. After it passes, Chilean labour law hands the union the right to vote on a strike.

What The Last Deal Paid

In August 2023 the two sides signed a 36-month contract after six days of mediation by the regional labour office in Antofagasta. The package included a closing bonus of CLP 17.8 million.

That is about US$19,200 at 927.5 pesos to the dollar on August 19, 2026. There were also soft loans worth CLP 3 million, roughly US$3,200.

Those are the numbers the supervisors now want to beat.

Why Escondida Strikes Move World Markets

Escondida sits in the Atacama Desert and is run by BHP, which holds 57.5%. Meanwhile Rio Tinto owns 30% and Japan’s JECO group the rest.

The mine produced 1.3 million tonnes of copper in BHP’s 2025 financial year, its best in 17 years. Chile as a whole mined about 5.4 million tonnes in 2025, close to a quarter of world supply.

The 2017 Strike Everyone Still Remembers

In February 2017 the operators’ union walked out and stayed out for roughly six weeks. Chilean accounts put it at 44 days, the longest stoppage the country’s private mining sector had seen.

Mining. com reported the mine lost more than 120,000 tonnes of copper.

In the end the union invoked Article 369 of the old labour code. That extended the old contract for 18 months, so workers returned with no new deal and no bonus.

And The Short, Expensive Strike Of 2024

The pattern changed in 2024. Sindicato N°1, with about 2,400 members, downed tools on Tuesday, August 13, and had a preliminary accord by Friday.

Reuters put the final package at around US$32,000 a worker plus US$2,000 in low-interest loans, on a three-year contract. Three days of stoppage bought far more than 44 days had in 2017.

Copper Prices Are Doing The Union A Favour

Cash copper on the London Metal Exchange set a record US$14,912 a tonne on August 17, 2026. In fact a squeeze in the London market drove it there.

The three-month benchmark was trading nearer US$13,900 a tonne by August 19. That leaves copper up around 14% so far this year.

Meanwhile BHP reported underlying attributable profit of US$13.2 billion for the year to June 2026, up 30%. In addition, copper overtook iron ore as its biggest earner for the first time.

The Awkward Part: Output Is About To Fall

BHP is not negotiating from a position of pure strength. Escondida president Alejandro Tapia said in August that the mine enters a temporary production valley.

As a result, output will be 1.0 to 1.1 million tonnes in its 2027 financial year. That is a drop of up to 300,000 tonnes, caused by falling ore grades.

A new concentrator costing an estimated US$4.4 billion to US$5.15 billion is meant to reverse it later.

Lundin Cuts Its Caserones Forecast After A Second Storm

Further south in the same desert, a very different problem hit another Chilean copper mine. Lundin Mining said on August 19 that a second severe winter storm in the Atacama region had damaged Caserones again.

The first storm knocked out power at the mine from July 18 to July 30. Then a storm that began on August 13 re-damaged a transmission tower, and power failed again on August 14.

The New Numbers From Lundin

Caserones now expects 120,000 to 130,000 tonnes of copper in 2026, down from 130,000 to 140,000 tonnes. Cash costs rise to US$2.15-US$2.35 a pound from US$2.05-US$2.25.

Company-wide guidance falls to 300,000-325,000 tonnes from 310,000-335,000 tonnes. Candelaria, Lundin’s other Chilean mine, is still expected to hit its target.

What To Watch Next

Chief executive Jack Lundin said crews were restoring power and reopening access roads, with full power expected within days. Even so, the company had kept its forecast unchanged after the first storm, and only cut once the second one landed.

For Escondida, the next milestone is BHP’s answer and then the countdown to September 30. Talks at the mine have gone to the wire before.

Both a 44-day walkout and a three-day one are live in everyone’s memory.

Background: Chile Inflation Holds Flat in June but Annual Rate Climbs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which union is negotiating at Escondida in 2026?

Sindicato N°2 de Supervisores de Minera Escondida, the supervisors’ union, which has 1,020 members. The larger operators’ union, Sindicato N°1, is not at the table this time.

When could a strike happen?

The current contract expires on September 30, 2026. Under Chilean law a strike vote only becomes possible once bargaining stalls near that deadline, so nothing can happen before then.

How much did Escondida workers win in 2024?

Reuters reported a package worth about US$32,000 per worker, plus US$2,000 in low-interest loans. The three-year contract was signed in August 2024 after a three-day strike.

How big is the Lundin Mining production cut at Caserones?

Lundin trimmed 2026 copper guidance at Caserones by 10,000 tonnes at each end of the range, to 120,000-130,000 tonnes. Two winter storms cut power to the mine.

Sources: Diario Financiero; BioBioChile; Lundin Mining; Reuters; Mining.com; BHP.

World.title: Argentina Ships First Offshore Pipes for Vaca Muerta Oil Pipeline
World.content:
Argentina · Energy

Key Facts — The shipment The vessel Navvik Launcher loaded the first 99 subsea pipes at San Antonio Este, Rio Negro, from Thursday, August 13.

— The supplier SIAT, the Tenaris welded-pipe business, provided the steel; over 10,100 tonnes moved out of Dock Sud, Buenos Aires.

— The coating Of the 721 pipes now stockpiled in Patagonia, 658 carry a concrete jacket applied at the Socotherm plant in Escobar.

— The line 437 kilometres from Allen to Punta Colorada, about US$3 billion, starting at 180,000 barrels a day and scaling to 550,000.

— The southern bet YPF is preparing a fresh exploration campaign at Palermo Aike in Santa Cruz for November or December 2026.

The buried 437-kilometre line is already finished. The sea leg and its two mooring buoys are now the part that decides when Argentina can load its first export tanker.

Illustrative photo: the subsea pipelay vessel Seven Navica, of the type used to lay offshore lines. At Punta Colorada, the specialised vessel Seminole will lay about five kilometres of concrete-coated pipe out to two mooring buoys. (Photo: JoachimKohler-HB, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The first steel for the underwater stretch of Argentina’s Vaca Muerta oil pipeline has finally left port. A supply vessel loaded 99 pipes at San Antonio Este and set course for Punta Colorada, on the Atlantic coast.

After that short hop, the country’s biggest private energy project starts building the part that touches the sea.

What Actually Left the Dock

The vessel is called the Navvik Launcher, and it is the first of nine platform supply ships booked for this job. Loading began at one in the afternoon on Thursday, August 13, at the port of San Antonio Este.

It carried 99 pipes toward the works area off Sierra Grande, in Rio Negro province. Diario Rio Negro reported on August 19 that the load was complete and the first batch had sailed.

Those 99 are a small slice of a much bigger pile. In June, the bulk carrier MV Athanasia delivered 721 steel pipes to the same port.

They have been stacked there ever since.

Why These Pipes Are Not Ordinary Pipes

Of the 721 tubes, 658 wear a thick concrete jacket. That coating was applied at the Socotherm plant in Escobar, in Buenos Aires province, before the steel went back to the docks.

Concrete does two jobs at once here. It shields the steel from the seabed.

It also adds weight, so the line will not float or shift in the currents of the Golfo San Matias.

The Long Chain Behind One Boat Trip

The pipe itself came from SIAT, the welded-pipe business Tenaris runs in Argentina from Valentin Alsina, near Buenos Aires. More than 10,100 tonnes of it was shipped out of the public wharf at Dock Sud.

Loginter handled storage and stowage at Dock Sud, while Arendal coordinated the sea transport. So a single 99-pipe sailing sits on top of months of mill work, coating and warehousing.

That matters for a country trying to build local supply chains. Because the steel, the coating and the logistics were all Argentine, the project keeps much of its spending at home.

The Vaca Muerta Oil Pipeline in Plain Numbers

The line runs 437 kilometres from Allen, in Rio Negro, to a new terminal at Punta Colorada. YPF has put the total cost of pipeline plus terminal at about US$2.98 billion, which most reports round to US$3 billion.

The buried trunk line is 30 inches across. Near the coast and out under the water, the pipe widens to 38 inches, with 24-inch branches feeding each offshore loading point.

Techint said on August 14 that all 437 kilometres were built, after a pressure test on the Rio Negro crossing. Even so, the wider project was still running at roughly 77 to 80 percent in mid-August.

What Waits at Punta Colorada

The terminal will hold six tanks of 120,000 cubic metres each. Two CALM monobuoys, moored offshore, will let very large crude carriers load without coming alongside a jetty.

The subsea line between the tanks and the buoys is only about five kilometres long. Still, it is the piece that turns a Patagonian pipeline into an export business.

The buoys themselves are built in the United Arab Emirates and shipped out through the Strait of Hormuz. YPF chief executive Horacio Marin said in August that the second unit was already at sea.

The Offshore Fleet Is Assembling

A jack-up platform, the Combifloat C7, took position off Punta Colorada in the second week of August. It will support the work of joining the pipe on the seabed.

Meanwhile the pipelay vessel Seminole is being prepared in Bahia Blanca, after arriving on a semi-submersible heavy-lift ship. Once ready, it will lay the concrete-coated line out to the buoys.

When the First Tanker Sails

YPF told a congressional committee in late July that the first cargo should leave between the end of 2026 and early 2027. Several Argentine outlets now lean toward the early-2027 end of that window.

The system starts at about 180,000 barrels a day. It is designed to climb to 550,000 barrels a day during 2027 and, on company projections, to 700,000 by 2028.

That ramp is the whole point. Vaca Muerta output has outgrown existing export routes.

So a second Atlantic outlet decides how fast Argentina can sell its crude.

Who Owns It and Who Paid

The vehicle, VMOS S.A., groups YPF with Vista, Pan American Energy, Pampa Energia, Chevron, Pluspetrol, Shell, Tecpetrol and Neuquen’s GyP. YPF holds about 30 percent.

Financing leaned on a syndicated loan of roughly US$2 billion from international banks. Argentine reports call it the largest commercial infrastructure credit in the country’s history.

The project is also registered under the RIGI incentive regime for large investments.

The Objection Nobody Has Settled

Not everyone welcomes the terminal. UNESCO has asked Argentina for more environmental information about the works, because of the protected marine area nearby.

The deadline is February 2027. The Golfo San Matias is a calving ground for southern right whales.

Therefore the offshore campaign is being watched closely by conservation groups as well as by traders.

YPF Also Turns to the Younger Sister

While the coast fills with ships, YPF is reviving a very different bet in the far south. Palermo Aike, in Santa Cruz province, is the shale formation Argentine officials call the younger sister of Vaca Muerta.

The province’s first unconventional well, MAYPA. x-1, was drilled by YPF with partner CGC.

It went 3,500 metres down and 1,000 metres sideways, and cost around US$50 million. A production test of about 180 days is under way.

ADNSUR reported on August 15 that YPF is preparing a new exploration campaign there, with work starting in November or December. CGC owner Eduardo Eurnekian has put the play’s potential at up to 10 billion barrels of oil.

He also cites more than 130 trillion cubic feet of gas. Those numbers are company estimates, not certified reserves.

Santa Cruz’s energy minister, Jaime Alvarez, prefers a softer line, calling Palermo Aike possibly half a Vaca Muerta.

What to Watch Next

The next milestones are physical and easy to track. Eight more supply-ship runs will move the rest of the 721 pipes.

Then the Seminole must start laying, and the second monobuoy has to be anchored. Only after those steps does a tanker date become real.

Until then, the finished 437 kilometres of buried steel are a very expensive line waiting on five kilometres of seabed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Vaca Muerta oil pipeline?

It is a 437-kilometre crude line, known as VMOS. It runs from Allen in Rio Negro to a new export terminal at Punta Colorada.

Who supplied the pipes for the offshore section?

SIAT, the Argentine welded-pipe business of Tenaris. More than 10,100 tonnes were shipped from Dock Sud, and 658 of the 721 pipes were concrete-coated at Socotherm in Escobar.

When will Argentina export oil through Punta Colorada?

YPF has guided to a window between late 2026 and early 2027, and recent Argentine reporting leans toward early 2027. The system starts near 180,000 barrels a day.

What is the younger sister of Vaca Muerta?

Palermo Aike, a shale formation in Santa Cruz province. YPF drilled the first unconventional well there with CGC and plans a new exploration campaign starting in November or December 2026.

Sources: Diario Rio Negro; ArgenPorts; GlobalPorts; Techint; Infobae; ADNSUR.

World.title: Argentina Beef Consumption Falls to Its Lowest in Over Two Decades
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts — The number 46.3 kilos of beef per person a year, measured over the 12 months to July 2026, according to CICCRA.

— The fall down 9.4% from 51.1 kilos a year earlier, or 4.8 kilos less on every plate.

— The supply squeeze domestic beef supply between January and July dropped about 12%, some 163,400 tonnes less than in 2025.

— The price beef cost roughly 52% more in July than a year before, with butcher shops up 56.6%, per IPCVA.

— The bright spots lamb exports rose 34% by volume in the first half, and Panama opened to four Argentine citrus fruits.

Chicken has quietly overtaken beef on the national plate, while lamb exports jump and Panama opens its door to Argentine citrus.

Illustrative photo: an Argentine asado grill with beef cuts, chicken and sausages beside a stack of firewood. Beef consumption has fallen to 46.3 kilos per person a year, the lowest in over two decades. (Photo: Robertaleotta2020, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Argentina beef consumption has slipped to 46.3 kilos per person a year, the lowest reading in more than two decades. That figure covers the 12 months to July 2026 and comes from CICCRA, the country’s meat industry chamber.

Argentines are now eating 4.8 kilos less beef each than they did a year ago.

The Number Behind the Argentina Beef Consumption Slide

CICCRA publishes a rolling 12-month average, so the series smooths out seasonal noise. Its July 2026 reading came in at 46.3 kilos per person, against 51.1 kilos a year earlier.

That is a 9.4% drop, and the chamber called it a historic low. Argentina beef consumption has not been this thin since the early 2000s.

The wider supply picture is starker still. Between January and July, the domestic market absorbed 1.202 million tonnes of beef.

About 12% less than in the same stretch of 2025.

Why the Fall Happened So Fast

Price did most of the work. Beef in the Buenos Aires area cost around 52% more in July 2026 than in July 2025.

According to the IPCVA beef promotion institute. Butcher shops pushed hardest, at 56.6% year on year, while supermarkets rose 43.3%.

Prices did steady over four months, yet the damage to household budgets was already done. Wages have been recovering, but not fast enough to close that gap.

Because beef climbed further than almost anything else in the basket, families simply bought less of it.

Chicken Overtakes Beef on the National Plate

For a country built on the asado, this is the headline shift. Chicken consumption now sits near 49 to 50 kilos per person a year, according to figures from CEPA and industry data.

That puts poultry ahead of beef for the first time in the statistical record. Pork has climbed too, from about 6 kilos per person twenty years ago to roughly 19 kilos today.

The reason is arithmetic, not taste. Chicken prices rose about 30% over the year, barely half the pace of beef, so shoppers switched.

Total meat consumption has held up better than beef alone. Argentines still eat plenty of protein overall, so the change is about which animal, not how much.

Fewer Cattle, Less Meat

Supply tightened as well. Argentina slaughtered 7.09 million head of cattle between January and July 2026, down 9.8% from a year earlier.

Beef output over the same seven months reached 1.689 million tonnes, a 6.8% decline. Producers have been holding back females to rebuild herds, which trims short-term supply.

Carcass weights did rise, softening the blow. Even so, less meat reached the counter while demand for it was already sagging.

Exports Take a Bigger Slice

A shrinking herd is now feeding a growing export book. Shipments between January and July hit 487,200 tonnes carcass equivalent, up 8.8% year on year.

That means roughly 30% of production went abroad, against about a quarter a year earlier. In the first half alone, Argentina sold 280,140 tonnes for about US$2.26 billion.

Analysts expect full-year beef exports above US$3 billion. Since foreign buyers pay in dollars, packers naturally chase them first.

Cheaper Beef Starts Arriving From Brazil

Something unusual is happening at the same time. Argentina, a byword for beef, is importing more of it, mostly from Brazil.

Purchases of Brazilian beef reached about 13,700 tonnes in the first half, up 122% by volume. That is still only around 1.3% of domestic consumption, so the shift is a trend rather than a takeover.

Industry voices describe a slow move toward the Uruguayan model. In short, import cheaper cuts for the home market and send premium local beef overseas.

Lamb Exports Jump 34%

Away from the beef counter, one Argentine meat is booming. Sheep meat exports rose 34% by volume in the first half of 2026, the Agriculture Secretariat reported in mid-August.

Shipments totalled 4,669,757 kilos of product weight, against 3,497,311 kilos a year earlier. Export earnings climbed 46%, and average value per tonne rose 10%.

The European Union remains the main buyer, with Middle Eastern markets growing. Argentina now has 44 open destinations for sheep meat, most of it raised in Patagonia.

Sheep farming remains small next to cattle, yet the growth matters for southern provinces. Santa Cruz and Chubut supply much of the flock behind those shipments.

Panama Opens to Argentine Citrus

The other piece of good news came from Central America. Panama agreed phytosanitary terms for four fresh Argentine citrus fruits in August 2026.

The list covers lemons, mandarins, oranges and grapefruit. Argentina’s Agriculture Secretariat handled the deal through SENASA, its food safety agency, with Panama’s agriculture ministry MIDA.

Panama published the rules as resolutions DNSV 427 to 430 of 2026. Tucumán, the world’s largest lemon producer, stands to gain most, although neither government published a volume target.

What This Means for Visitors and Residents

If you are eating out in Buenos Aires, the steak is still excellent. The difference is what it costs relative to everything else on the menu.

Parrillas have leaned harder on chicken, pork and cheaper cuts. Meanwhile many households now save beef for weekends instead of weekdays.

Restaurant menus tell the same story. Cheaper cuts and chicken dishes have spread, while the premium steaks increasingly target visitors paying in dollars.

What to Watch Next

Two things will decide whether the slide continues. The first is whether real wages keep gaining ground on food prices through the rest of 2026.

The second is the cattle cycle. Once herd rebuilding ends, more animals should reach market, and that extra supply could finally cool prices at the counter.

Imports are the wild card. If Brazilian beef keeps arriving at lower prices, it could put a ceiling on what Argentine butchers can charge.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much beef do Argentines eat now?

About 46.3 kilos per person a year, measured over the 12 months to July 2026. That is 4.8 kilos less than a year earlier, and the lowest figure in more than two decades.

Who publishes the Argentina beef consumption figure?

CICCRA, the Argentine chamber of meat industry and commerce, publishes a monthly report with a rolling 12-month per-capita average. Infobae and other outlets carried the July 2026 reading on 19 August 2026.

Is chicken really more popular than beef in Argentina?

Yes, by volume. Chicken now runs at roughly 49 to 50 kilos per person a year.

Which citrus fruits can Argentina now send to Panama?

Lemons, mandarins, oranges and grapefruit. Panama approved the phytosanitary requirements in resolutions DNSV 427 to 430 of 2026, after talks between SENASA and Panama’s MIDA.

Sources: Infobae; CICCRA; La Nación; IPCVA; Agritotal.

World.title: Argentina Digital Health Plan Lands US$700 Million IDB Credit Line
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts — The headline number a conditional credit line of up to US$700 million with the Inter-American Development Bank, approved by Decree 757/2026.

— The date the decree was signed on August 18, 2026 and published in Argentina’s official gazette on August 19, 2026.

— The borrower the Argentine Republic, not a state bank; provinces receive the money through individual loans.

— The first loan US$85 million for Mendoza’s public hospital network, with disbursements planned over four years.

— The second loan up to US$60 million approved on August 10, 2026 for Rio Negro, aimed at about 320,000 public-system patients.

The first US$85 million goes to Mendoza, and the province has already warned the cash has not landed yet.

Illustrative photo: the Hospital Central and FUESMEN complex in Mendoza, the province set to receive the first US$85 million loan under the US$700 million credit line. (Photo: Federico Gomez Aghetta, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Argentina Digital Health spending is about to get a large foreign credit line. A presidential decree published on August 19 approves a framework worth up to US$700 million with the Inter-American Development Bank.

The money is meant to drag provincial hospital systems out of paper files and into shared digital records.

What Argentina Actually Signed Off On

Decree 757/2026 approves the model agreement for a conditional credit line numbered AR-O0033. The lender is the Inter-American Development Bank, known in the region as the BID.

The ceiling is US$700 million. However, the decree does not hand over a single cheque, because a conditional credit line works more like an approved overdraft.

Why the Argentina Digital Health Line Is Not One Big Loan

A conditional credit line is an umbrella. Individual loans are then carved out of it, one at a time, each with its own contract and its own conditions.

The umbrella stays open for ten years from the day the agreement takes effect. As a result, provinces can queue up over a decade rather than compete in a single round.

Mendoza Is First in the Queue

The same decree authorises the first individual loan, worth US$85 million, for Mendoza. It funds a project with a very literal name: the Consolidation of the Digital Transformation of the Provincial Health System.

Local reporting says the money will be drawn down over four years and repaid over 25. Interest is tied to SOFR, the dollar benchmark that replaced Libor.

Approved Money Is Not Arrived Money

In mid-August, Mendoza folded the operation into its 2026 budget. Even so, the province spelled out that the accounting entry did not mean the dollars had landed.

That distinction matters across the whole package. Board approval, a decree, a signed contract and an actual disbursement are four different milestones.

And only the first two have clearly happened.

Rio Negro Is Already Second

On August 10, 2026, the bank’s board approved up to US$60 million for Rio Negro. Coverage of the operation describes it as the second project under the same digital health line.

The stated goal is to reach roughly 320,000 people who rely only on the public network. In addition, the loan is set to cover the entire cost of that provincial programme.

What the Money Buys Inside a Hospital

The Argentina Digital Health shopping list is unglamorous and, for patients, quite useful. It covers electronic medical records, appointment systems, laboratory and imaging software, connectivity and cybersecurity.

Telemedicine sits alongside all of that. Because Argentine provinces are enormous and thinly populated in places, a remote consultation can replace a very long drive.

Why Provinces Do the Spending

Argentina runs health care through 24 jurisdictions: 23 provinces plus the city of Buenos Aires. Each one owns its hospitals, hires its staff and buys its own software.

That is why a national credit line has to be sliced into provincial loans. The federal government signs as guarantor, with provincial revenue-sharing transfers standing behind the promise.

Who Borrows, and a Common Mix-Up

The borrower here is the Argentine Republic. The country’s state development bank, BICE, is not a party to this credit line, despite occasional confusion in early summaries.

BICE has been busy with its own peso lending instead, including leasing and small-business facilities announced during 2026. Those programmes are separate from the multilateral loan described in the decree.

Two Other Rule Changes Landed the Same Fortnight

On August 6, the Central Bank issued Communication A 8464. It lets local insurers covering projects under the large-investment incentive regime buy foreign currency to pay reinsurance premiums abroad.

The access is narrow, not general. Insurers must use funds transferred by the project vehicle from its own foreign borrowing, and must act within 72 business hours.

A New Register for Mining Investors

Also published on August 19, Resolution 68/2026 from the Mining Secretariat creates the Mining Investment Registry, or RIM. It replaces the annex of a 2018 resolution and moves filings onto the state’s remote-paperwork platform.

Every beneficiary is identified by tax number, and every declared project gets a unique code. Since the registry also handles single-project vehicles, it links the older mining law to the newer incentive regime.

The Wider Lending Relationship

The health line is not an isolated cheque. In 2026 the bank has also approved US$500 million for Argentina’s targeted energy subsidy system and US$300 million for public administration modernisation.

Those operations follow the same pattern of long tenors and SOFR-linked pricing. Overall, the lender is financing plumbing rather than headline projects, which is slow work and rarely makes front pages.

What to Watch Next

Three things will show whether this is real. First, the signed loan contracts; second, the first disbursement dates; third, which province is chosen third.

Demand for public care is rising. Since the share of Argentines with no union or private health plan has grown in recent years.

Therefore the queue for these provincial loans is unlikely to stay short.

Background: Fintechs and Digital Banks in Brazil 2026: Market Guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is Argentina borrowing for digital health?

Up to US$700 million, as a framework credit line with the Inter-American Development Bank. Individual loans are then approved one by one, so the full amount is a ceiling rather than a transfer.

Has any money been paid out yet?

No disbursement has been reported. Mendoza’s US$85 million loan was written into the provincial budget in August 2026.

Is BICE, the state development bank, the borrower?

No. The borrower is the Argentine Republic, and provinces are the beneficiaries. BICE runs its own separate credit programmes and is not part of this agreement.

What will patients notice from the Argentina Digital Health programme?

Mainly shared electronic records, easier appointments and more telemedicine. Rio Negro’s programme alone targets about 320,000 people who depend only on public hospitals and clinics.

Sources: Boletin Oficial de la Republica Argentina; El Cronista; Infobae; El Sol (Mendoza); Devdiscourse; Uxolo.

World.title: Brazil Electoral Fund Frees US$440 Million in Public Campaign Money
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts — The release Brazil’s top electoral court freed R$2.3 billion (about US$440 million) on August 18, 2026.

— The trigger the Workers’ Party (PT) dropped its own lawsuit, and the court closed the case without ruling on it.

— The slice that R$2.3 billion is the 48% share split by how many federal deputies each party holds.

— The whole pot the 2026 fund is R$4,961,519,777, roughly US$950 million, shared by 30 parties.

— The clock campaigning began August 16, and parties must pass the cash to candidates by August 30.

The unlocked slice is one piece of a nearly US$950 million pot that taxpayers hand political parties before the October 4 vote.

Brazil Electoral Fund Frees US$440 Million in Public Campaign Money. (Photo internet reproduction)

Money from the Brazil Electoral Fund is moving again. On August 18, 2026, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) released R$2.3 billion, about US$440 million, to political parties.

The payment had been frozen for days because the Workers’ Party (PT) was suing over how its own share was calculated.

What the Brazil Electoral Fund Actually Is

Brazilian campaigns run mostly on public money. Companies were banned from donating in 2015, and Congress replaced them in 2017 with a taxpayer-funded pot.

That pot is the Fundo Especial de Financiamento de Campanha, or FEFC. In English it is simply the Brazil Electoral Fund, and every real inside it comes from the federal budget.

Why the Payment Got Stuck

The court had already published each party’s number on July 1. Yet the biggest chunk of the money never left the account.

On August 13, minister Estela Aranha asked to review the PT case, which paused the judgment. As a result, R$2.3 billion sat frozen for every party, not just the PT.

Other parties could only wait. Because the 48% band is calculated as one block, a dispute over one party’s seat count froze everyone’s transfer.

The Fight Was Over a Single Deputy

The PT did not attack the formula. Instead, it argued that its bench in the Chamber of Deputies should count 69 members rather than 68.

The extra name was Paulão, a PT deputy from Alagoas. He lost his seat after a 2022 vote recount.

Although a May 2026 order from Supreme Court minister Dias Toffoli suspended that process.

How the Court Closed the Case

TSE president Kassio Nunes Marques, who was also the case rapporteur, voted against the party. He held that Toffoli’s order paused the proceeding but did not force a fresh recount.

The PT then withdrew the petition. On August 18 the full court unanimously accepted the withdrawal and shut the case without judging the merits.

There was a second reason to give up. On August 12, Supreme Court minister Cristiano Zanin rejected Paulão’s separate bid to recover his mandate.

How the Cash Is Divided

The split is written into Brazil’s election law and leaves the court almost no discretion. Two percent goes equally to every registered party, so even tiny ones get something.

After that, 35% follows votes cast for the Chamber, 48% follows the number of federal deputies, and 15% follows Senate seats. The 48% band is the piece that was blocked.

Who Takes Home the Most

The Liberal Party (PL), which backs the Bolsonaro camp, leads with roughly R$881.7 million, near US$169 million. The PT follows with about R$615.4 million, or some US$118 million.

União Brasil takes around R$526.2 million (US$101 million), the PSD about R$421 million (US$81 million). And the PP roughly R$417.1 million (US$80 million).

Together those five hold 57.68% of the fund. Small parties are not left empty-handed.

The 2% equal share guarantees each of the 30 registered parties a floor. Although it is a rounding error next to the PL’s total.

What the Money Can Buy

Spending limits were kept at 2022 levels and only adjusted for inflation. A presidential campaign may spend up to R$88.9 million in the first round, close to US$17 million.

A runoff adds R$44.4 million more, near US$8.5 million. Governor races in São Paulo are capped at R$26.6 million, while a federal deputy may spend roughly R$3.2 million, near US$610,000.

Those ceilings cover the obvious costs. Rallies, sound trucks, printed material, marketing teams and paid social media boosts all come out of the same pot.

Why Brazilians Call It the Fundão

Critics use the nickname fundão, meaning the big fund, and the arithmetic explains why. Divided by 158,745,463 registered voters, the fund costs roughly R$31 a head, about US$6.

Lawmakers set the amount themselves. In October 2025, the budget committee lifted the 2026 figure from R$1 billion to R$4.9 billion.

Moving R$2.9 billion away from parliamentary earmarks.

The Argument on the Other Side

Defenders say the alternative was worse. Before 2015, construction giants bankrolled campaigns, and the Lava Jato scandal showed what those favors bought.

Public money is also easier to police. Because the court controls the flow, it can force parties to send at least 30% of the fund to women candidates.

There is a practical argument too. Public funding is traceable, so auditors can follow each transfer instead of chasing hidden company favours.

The Fund Is Shrinking in Real Terms

The headline number looks frozen in time. The FEFC has stayed near R$4.9 billion since 2022, even though prices have climbed since then.

A separate permanent pot, the fundo partidário, adds R$1.43 billion a year for party running costs. That is another US$274 million, paid monthly whether or not there is an election.

Wealthy donors have not disappeared. Individuals may still give up to 10% of their previous year’s income, which keeps a private lane open beside the public one.

What Happens Next

Parties must now hand the money to candidates. The general deadline is August 30, while transfers tied to the quotas for women, Black and Indigenous candidates run to September 8.

Voting is on October 4, with any runoff four weeks later. Since the campaign opened on August 16, the released cash arrives just as television and online advertising begin in earnest.

Leftover money does not stay with the parties. Campaign accounts are audited by the court, and unused public funds must be reported and returned rather than pocketed.

Background: Lula 39%, Flávio Bolsonaro 33% — Brazil’s Race in the July Polls.

Background: Brazil Tax Reform Timeline: Tech Sector Faces 2026 Invoice Shock.

Background: Fintechs and Digital Banks in Brazil 2026: Market Guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much was released and when?

The TSE released R$2.3 billion, about US$440 million, on August 18, 2026. It is the 48% slice of the campaign fund tied to the size of each party’s bench in the Chamber of Deputies.

What was the Workers’ Party suing about?

The PT wanted its Chamber bench counted as 69 deputies instead of 68, which would have lifted its share. It dropped the case, and the court closed it without ruling.

How big is the whole fund?

The 2026 Brazil Electoral Fund totals R$4,961,519,777, roughly US$950 million at R$5.22 to the dollar. Thirty parties share it, and the top five take 57.68%.

Where does the money come from?

The federal budget. Congress sets the amount each year, and the fund exists because the Supreme Court banned corporate donations in 2015.

Sources: Tribunal Superior Eleitoral; Folha de S.Paulo; O Globo; Estadão; CartaCapital.

World.title: Brazil Election Polls: Big Leads in Brasília and São Paulo
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts — The Brasília governor race Real Time Big Data puts Celina Leão on 34%, José Roberto Arruda on 22% and Leandro Grass on 18%.

— The Brasília Senate race Michelle Bolsonaro leads on 25%, ahead of Leila Barros on 17%, with Bia Kicis and Erika Kokay tied on 15%.

— The runoff caveat Flávio Bolsonaro 44% to Lula 39% is a Federal District result from 1,600 local voters, not a national poll.

— The São Paulo race Paraná Pesquisas has Governor Tarcísio de Freitas on 50% and Fernando Haddad on 33.8%, a gap of just over 16 points.

— The method Brasília fieldwork ran 14-18 August with a 2-point error margin; São Paulo ran 16-18 August with 2.4 points.

The eye-catching Flavio Bolsonaro lead over Lula comes from Brasília alone, a right-leaning enclave, not from Brazil as a whole.

Illustrative photo: Celina Leão at a Brasília government ceremony handing over police vehicles. She leads the Federal District governor race with 34% in the Real Time Big Data survey of 14-18 August 2026. (Photo: Agência Brasília, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)
