World.title: Can a New ‘European Confederation’ Reconnect the UK with the EU?
World.content:
Nick Boles, a former Conservative MP and UK minister, made a big splash in a country still struggling to adapt to the consequences of Brexit when he published an essay this month proposing a new deal for the United Kingdom’s relationship with Europe. By Europe, Boles primarily means the European Union and European Economic Area (EEA) countries, Switzerland, Ukraine and the Western Balkans.

His proposal sparked reactions from international media and several commentators in the Western Balkans, but it also generated false claims that this was a proposal by the new UK government under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Central to Boles’s proposal is the negotiation of a 'New Deal' between the UK and Europe and the establishment of a new European Confederation that would replace the European Political Community (EPC), a 47-member intergovernmental forum established in 2022 in response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The diagnosis of the UK’s current predicament is accurate. Its post-Brexit relationship with Europe remains unresolved, while weakening transatlantic ties and a gradual US strategic shift away from Europe increases space for threats from Russia and China.

World.title: Suspend Officers Suspected of Beating Serb, Kosovo Police Inspectorate Says
World.content:
Kosovo Police Inspectorate. Photo: BIRN

Kosovo’s Police Inspectorate (IPK) said on Tuesday that it had recommended the suspension of two officers following an investigation into allegations made by Nenad Raskovic, a Kosovo Serb, on August 11.

Raskovic has alleged that he was physically assaulted by police officers during a raid on his home in the village of Dren, near the northern municipality of Zubin Potok. The inspectorate launched its investigation on August 12 following media reports about the incident.

Photographs shared in the media and on social networks show injuries on Raskovic’s back.

“Today [Tuesday], the IPK recommended that the Kosovo Police suspend two police officers from the North Mitrovica Regional Police Directorate, suspected of being involved in this case in connection with the criminal offence of ‘mistreatment in the exercise of official duties or public authority’,” the inspectorate said in a statement.

The IPK, an independent institution overseeing police conduct, said further investigative activities will be carried out in cooperation with the Basic Prosecution in Mitrovica “to establish the full circumstances of the incident and determine the actions of the police officers involved”.

The Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party Srpska Lista said on August 11 that Raskovic reported that police officers entered his home in Dren during a raid and, after searching the property, began beating him without explanation.

“After that, Nenad was left tied to a tree. With the help of friends, he was freed and taken to the Family Medical Centre in Zubin Potok, and then to the Clinical Hospital Centre in Mitrovica,” said Srpska Lista.

Raskovic also made these allegations while speaking to the media from the hospital. He was later sent to Belgrade for further treatment.

The Kosovo Police confirmed that Raskovic’s home was among the properties searched during an operation. Erduan Baliqi, a police spokesperson, told BIRN that the searches were conducted as part of an operation related to information about weapons.

Srpska Lista called on Western embassies and international organisations, as well as NATO-led KFOR peacekeepers and the EU rule-of-law mission EULEX, to examine the allegations and act within their respective mandates to establish the facts and ensure the rights and safety of the public.

Civil society organisations in northern Kosovo, where Serbs form the majority, have also called on the European Union to assess EULEX’s monitoring of the Kosovo Police.

World.title: ‘Terror-Free Turkey’ Process Could Boost Ankara’s International Status
World.content:
Turkey’s attempt to bring four decades of conflict with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) to an end is usually discussed primarily as a domestic political question. Understandably, the process named by Ankara as “Terror-Free Turkey” is framed around internal security, disarmament and the future relationship between the Turkish state and its Kurdish citizens. Yet such a reading is incomplete.

The conflict with the PKK has never been merely an internal security challenge. For decades, it has shaped Turkey’s relations with Iraq and Syria, complicated its dealings with Washington and European governments and absorbed substantial military and intelligence resources.

The Turkish parliament’s adoption of the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration on August 10 must therefore also be understood as a development with potentially significant foreign policy consequences. Turkey will not automatically become more powerful if the process succeeds, but it could gain greater freedom to redistribute political, military and diplomatic attention across several theatres.

The central question is whether Ankara can convert a reduction in one of its longest running security burdens into greater regional room for manoeuvre. Foreign policy influence is never generated automatically by the disappearance of a single security problem. What remains decisive are economic resources, institutional quality, diplomatic credibility, military capabilities, alliance structures and the behaviour of other states.

World.title: Serbian Economy Braces for Ripple Effect of Danube Cargo Slowdown
World.content:
Severe drought has slowed cargo transport on the Serbian stretch of the Danube almost to a halt, impacting supply chains and likely driving up prices.

In July, Elixir Group, operator of one of the country’s main Danube ports, Prahovo, reported an increase of roughly 31 per cent year-on-year in the amount of cargo it handled. That all changed towards the end of the month, when the water level at Prahovo fell 45 centimetres between July 17 and August 18, forcing barge operators to drastically reduce the loads they carry.

“Due to conditions on the lower Danube, navigation has been completely suspended, directly preventing cargo vessels from reaching the Port of Prahovo,” said Dragan Stevovic, Elixir’s director of logistics and distribution, chemical division.

World.title: Russian Propaganda Thrives in Greek Media Via ‘Disinformation Laundering’
World.content:
A report splashed across Greek online media last month declared sensationally that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s parents were being investigated for corruption, after $11 million dollars was found in their bank accounts.

It wasn’t true and was debunked by Ellinika Hoaxes, a Greek fact-checking organisation. Yet the story wasn’t just published by fringe pro-Russian sites such as Pronews. It was also published by Newsbomb, a highly popular Greek-language site belonging to the DPG Digital Media Group. DPG is owned by Dimitris Giannakopoulos, a businessman and the owner of basketball club Panathinaikos BC, who is sympathetic to Vladimir Putin.

Some of the reports were accompanied by a video taken from a Russia-friendly X account which purported to be from Europe Today, a show from French pan-European TV news network, Euronews. But as Ellinika Hoaxes pointed out, the Euronews logo in the video is different from the regular one, which has a blue background and white letters and not a white background with blue letters.

In its debunking, Ellinika Hoaxes pointed out that the made-up Zelensky story was “yet another case of fabricated fake news” originating from a Russian disinformation network, Matryoshka. Also known as Operation Overload, Matryoshka is a coordinated Russian propaganda network that creates and spreads fake news and videos, deepfakes and memes using logos of well-known Western media outlets.

World.title: Serbian Media Outlets’ Management Change Sparks Suspicion Ahead of Elections
World.content:
In a move that has sparked widespread speculation across the media scene in Serbia, Portuguese media entrepreneur Pedro Vargas Santos David was registered as a director of four companies on Monday – Adria News, United Media Digital, Adria News Nova S, and Dan Graf.

The companies run the N1 and Nova S television stations in Serbia, news website Nova.rs, daily newspapers Nova and Danas, weekly magazine Radar and the Serbian edition of Forbes. These outlets’ directors were dismissed.

All of the media outlets operate within Adria News Network, owned by the Luxembourg-registered United Group. International investment group Alpac Capital and Summer Parent, the ultimate shareholder of United Group, initially confirmed back in May that an agreement had been reached for the sale of Adria News Network. Ownership changes have not been made yet.

World.title: Kosovo Opposition Snubs Acting President’s Meeting Amid Parliamentary Crisis
World.content:
Kosovo’s Acting President Albulena Haxhiu meets political leaders in Pristina on August 18, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s opposition on Tuesday disregarded an invitation from acting President Albulena Haxhiu to a meeting with the country’s political leaders aimed at defusing the ongoing parliamentary crisis.

The crisis centres around the inability of political parties to agree on a candidate for president. Under the constitution, failure to choose a new head of state will trigger new parliamentary elections.

However, attendees at Haxhiu’s meeting were mainly allies of her own party, Vetevendosje.

Instead of attending the meeting, a group of opposition MPs from the Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) and the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo (AAK) went to the Kosovo Assembly, as they have been doing every day, to put pressure on the provisional parliamentary speaker, Avni Dehari, to call the inaugural session of the Assembly.

The assembly’s rules require the provisional speaker to invite MPs to a session every 48 hours until they elect a speaker. But the last time Dehari actually presided over a session was August 8, which lasted only a few minutes.

Dehari insists he will not call a session until parties agreed on a new president.

“This situation should alarm all of us. No election victory gives anyone the right to put themselves above the constitution,” Besa Kabashi Ramaj, a PDK MP, told her opposition colleagues at a makeshift meeting in the Assembly.

Opposition MPs have been holding these makeshift meetings every day in an attempt to press Vetevendosje to call the inaugural session.

In elections in June, Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, putting them well ahead of the PDK, which won 22. The Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK) won 18 seats and has insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand.

Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority in the assembly to form a new government by again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved. The parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new assembly, otherwise a new election will be triggered.

Last week, LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku announced that his party is withdrawing its demand to hold the president’s post in order to ease the negotiations for the formation of new institutions. However, no meeting with Vetevendosje leader Kurti has been held since.

On Monday, Abdixhiku announced that he is not interested in attending Haxhiu’s meeting because opposition parties claim that Haxhiu’s role as acting president has ceased with the start of this Assembly’s session and that her role can be resumed only if she is re-elected as assembly speaker.

“The only meeting I could hold is with [Albin] Kurti. In our view, Haxhiu is only an MP, therefore we can talk only with those who are entitled to talk,” Abdixhiku said.

“[Kurti] told us that he will meet with LDK soon,” Haxhiu told media after Tuesday’s meeting.

“After all these months, we don’t need to guess what the lack of agreement would bring… If we don’t agree today, new elections do not guarantee that we will agree tomorrow,” Haxhiu said, referring to the possibility of new snap elections if the parties fail to choose a new president.

The parliamentary polls would be the fourth in less than two years.

World.title: Czech Human Rights Agenda Faces Conservative Pushback Under Babis Government
World.content:
Coordination under threat

The human rights agenda is inherently cross-sectoral. Human rights issues arise in healthcare, education, social affairs, criminal procedure and similar areas. If it were transferred to a single ministry, it would lose its inter-ministerial authority, as well as the ability to provide input on government-level work. At the same time, this area is subject to a number of international agreements and state commitments.

“Through the Office of the Government, we had the opportunity to amplify the voices of vulnerable groups, promote dialogue and encourage their participation in public policy-making,” says former commissioner Simackova Laurencikova. “We served as a forum for dialogue among civil society, non-governmental organizations, academia and government agencies, so that these people could genuinely meet, listen to one another and work together effectively. Not just alongside one another, but together.”

In Simackova Laurencikova’s view, this society-wide coordination has been the main reason for the significant progress made on the issue of domestic and sexual violence in recent years. “We succeeded in drafting and enacting a redefinition of rape and in drafting a new, comprehensive law on domestic violence, which, for the first time ever, establishes a uniform definition of what constitutes domestic violence,” she says.

According to Simackova Laurencikova, if officials find themselves in a subordinate position within a ministry, their bargaining power will be significantly curbed. “Let’s say you’re drafting an action plan pointing out that social service facilities are failing to adequately address the protection of the human rights of clients with intellectual disabilities. If the parent ministry then tells you, ‘No, we think the system is set up properly,’ then as a rank-and-file official in that ministry, you have no chance of getting the issue off the ground.”

She also cites a specific example from the past: “When the Ministry of Regional Development was drafting the Building Code, the requirement to make buildings and government offices accessible was omitted from all regulations. From our position at the Office of the Government, we had the opportunity to amplify the voices of vulnerable groups and set the dialogue on the right track.”

Prime Minister Babis has attempted to defend the reorganisation by citing a 2023 analysis by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) that assesses the state of the public administration. “Even the OECD says to consider placing councils that do not address a government’s priorities, or are not cross-sectoral, under individual ministries,” he said.

A closer reading of the analysis, however, shows that Babis’s interpretation omitted important context. While the document does allow for the transfer of certain specific councils, it in fact calls for strengthening the coordinating role directly under the Office of the Government when it comes to cross-sectoral issues, such as the human rights agenda. Furthermore, the OECD emphasised that any changes must be preceded by an in-depth analysis of effectiveness – an analysis that Babis’s cabinet failed to conduct.

Under pressure from experts, the prime minister finally agreed to a compromise: two new offices will be established within the Office of the Government: one for human rights and the protection of minorities, and one for mental health and addiction. Experts say, however, these will be merely empty shells.

“It will be more like a secretariat. It will lack specialised teams and capacity. All that will remain are secretaries who send out invitations and take minutes at meetings, but expertise on the legislative process, policy concepts and action plans will vanish from the Office of the Government for good,” warns Simackova Laurencikova.

According to information provided to iROZHLAS, even civil servants themselves have not had their concerns raised. “We still have questions about this. Honestly, I don’t know how it’s all going to work,” said one. At the same time, however, they said they considered the current discussions at the various ministries to be constructive, even if not all of them can be so described.

The cabinet’s actions drew an immediate reaction, both from officials and from experts serving on committees and working groups.

“As for advisory bodies such as committees and working groups, we know of dozens of people who have resigned at this stage or are seriously considering standing down. Some of them resigned immediately,” says Medal, spokesperson for Straka, the trade union organisation at the Office of the Government.

Anna Smyslova, another representative of the union, says some agencies are already completely paralysed, including the Committee for the Prevention of Domestic Violence and Violence Against Women. Yet this committee included key figures in the field; of 20 members, eight came directly from the non-profit sector, which provides direct assistance to victims.

Last week, Lucie Fukova, the government commissioner for Roma minority affairs, resigned from her post, citing her disagreement with the transfer of the Roma agenda to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs. Following her departure, Vice Chair Marian Dancso and member Tomas Scuka also stepped down as of the end of June. According to a statement provided to the Romea website, there are serious concerns that placing the agenda under the ministry will reduce Roma issues to a purely “social issue” and reinforce harmful stereotypes.

Towards the end of June, iROZHLAS repeatedly requested a statement from the current human rights commissioner, Tatana Mala. She did not respond to any calls, while her assistant, who could be reached by phone, stated that Mala was in meetings.

Only Justice Minister Jeronym Tejc of the ANO party replied, asserting that the equality agenda will not disappear. “The Ministry of Justice is not only in charge of criminal law legislation, but also civil legislation. I believe that where the equality agenda concerns the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, we will find common ground,” he said.

He added that when the agenda was located at the Office of the Government, the Ministry of Justice was also significantly involved in legislation related to domestic violence and the physical punishment of children.

World.title: Quiet Inheritance: Why the Croatian Diaspora Should Seek Citizenship For Their Children
World.content:
August the 19th, 2026 – Even if you don’t plan to open a business, move, or do anything concrete, as a member of the Croatian diaspora, gaining citizenship could mean the gateway to EU education and career opportunities for generations to come.

For a growing number of American parents who happen to have Croatian ancestry, the decision to pursue Croatian citizenship is no longer mainly about their own travel plans or personal connection to the country. It’s about their children…

eu citizenship is about so much more than getting through the border more quickly…

Across the United States, parents are quietly assembling birth certificates and family records. Maybe they were fuelled by the sense of sweeping national pride the World Cup brought, or maybe the fact that that burdensome double taxation treaty between the USA and Croatia is on its way to being scrapped. Maybe it’s none of that. It could be a desire to reconnect with the roots of their ancestors as a nod to all they went through for better lives across the Atlantic Ocean.

Whatever the reason behind the move, the end goal of such a move is relatively straightforward – to secure Croatian citizenship. Even if there are zero plans to move to Croatia or anywhere else in the EU, start up a business, move a company to the EU or retire, holding Croatian (and thus EU) citizenship means that their sons and daughters can also do the same, automatically gaining full EU rights. That of course includes unfettered access to higher education and unrestricted work opportunities across 27 different countries.

This isn’t just another theoretical benefit. Once a parent becomes a Croatian citizen through descent, minor children can typically acquire the same citizenship with far less complexity involved. That single step creates a permanent legal pathway that remains open for the next generation, regardless of whether the family ever relocates.

a european education with zero barriers

One of the clearest practical advantages is university access. EU citizens generally pay the same tuition rates as local students at public universities throughout most of the European Union. In many countries those fees are substantially lower than the costs American students face at home, and in some cases they approach zero for EU nationals. Holding a Croatian passport also removes the need for student visas or complex sponsorship arrangements when applying to programmes in Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Ireland, or other member states. Students can move freely for short courses, semester exchanges, or full degree programmes. The Erasmus network and similar mobility schemes become far more accessible when the student already holds EU citizenship rather than relying on temporary permissions.

For families watching American college costs rise astronomically year after year, this represents a concrete parallel option. It doesn’t require abandoning American universities. It simply expands the menu of realistic choices available to a teenager who holds both an American and a Croatian passport. It is also far easier on the pockets of parents who may only just be making ends meet.

career mobility following graduation – eu wide

The advantages continue after university is over and those famous photos are taken with diplomas in hand. An EU citizen can accept a job offer in any member state without needing a work permit or employer sponsorship. That flexibility matters in competitive fields where companies increasingly recruit across borders. Young dual citizens can take internships in Zagreb or just across the border in Ljubljana, accept graduate roles in Berlin or Amsterdam, or return home to the United States with the knowledge that EU opportunities remain permanently available to them whenever they get the itch to experience them.

Parents who secure the status of Croatian citizens while their children are still minors effectively hand them a form of professional insurance that is extremely difficult to obtain later in life. Rules can (and do) change. You only need to ask the Italian diaspora about the hurdles they now face in what was once an easy ride in getting Italian citizenship. Documentation becomes harder to locate and do anything with as older relatives pass away and time marches on. Completing the process now removes those future variables entirely and ensures flexibility that can hardly be matched in any other manner.

multi-generational safety

Many American parents with Croatian heritage say they have no intention of moving to Europe themselves. Nor do they need to. That’s totally irrelevant to the value of having Croatian citizenship for the next generation. The rights exist whether or not anyone relocates anywhere else. A family can remain fully based in the United States while still giving their children the legal ability to study, work, or live anywhere in the EU if they later choose to do so.

The same logic applies to grandchildren. Citizenship acquired today can, at least under current rules, be transmitted further down the line, creating a multi-generational safety net that requires just one single successful application at the starting point.

timing matters…

The administrative process for Croatian citizenship by descent is (in)famously document-heavy. Birth, marriage, and death records must be gathered, apostilled, and translated… The list goes on. That goes without even mentioning that much older records from the former Yugoslavia or earlier periods can take time to locate and deal with administratively. Consular and ministry processing times currently range from several months to well over a year depending on the complexity of the file.

Parents who begin while their own parents or grandparents are still able to help locate family documents often find the process smoother. Waiting until a child is already applying to universities can leave too little time for the citizenship to be finalised. For American families with verifiable Croatian ancestry, the window remains totally open. There is (at least for now) still no generational cutoff for eligible descendants in most descent-based cases, and dual citizenship with the United States is entirely permitted. The practical question is simply whether the family wants those EU education and mobility rights locked in for the next generation while the paperwork is still manageable.

The decision is less about returning to Croatia, less about business and investments, and more about giving children a permanent set of options that most of their American peers will never have. In an era of rising education costs and increasingly mobile careers, that quiet inheritance is proving more valuable than many families initially expected.

how croatianbydescent.com can help you get your hands on that trusty little blue passport

Croatian by Descent helps the diaspora to take that first step into the (sometimes choppy) waters of gaining Croatian citizenship. It acts as a complete guide to everything you might need to keep in mind when applying or just seeking more information. For total beginners with little to no knowledge of how administrative processes work in Croatia, this can be an invaluable source of guidance throughout the entire process.

Booking a free consultation with Croatian by Descent can set you on the path to securing Croatian and EU citizenship for yourself, thus making travelling to Croatia and Schengen for holidays easy and stress-free. It can also be a priceless gift to your children and grandchildren should they decide to take the leap (even temporarily) back to the country your ancestors left long ago, to attend higher education or to work, opening up a world of incredible opportunities that aren’t on the table for everyone.

World.title: Business Owners and Landlords Seek Relief After Fire in Omiš
World.content:
August the 19th, 2026 – Business owners and private landlords are seeking relief and compensation after the fire that has ravaged the Omiš area.

The well known association Glas poduzetnika (UGP – Voice of Entrepreneurs) has proposed that the Croatian Government adopt an emergency package of measures that would temporarily relieve entrepreneurs affected by the fire in the Omiš area of tax, tourism, chamber and local charges.

Poslovni reports that the association believes that assistance must not be limited only to those whose facilities physically burned down, because damage in the affected area is also suffered by those whose facilities remained intact but who, because of the fire, were left without guests, access, income or the possibility of regular business operations.

“Such a package of assistance should not have to be reinvented every time. Croatia needs a predefined model of automatic relief and assistance to the economy in the event of fires, floods, earthquakes and other major disasters. When a catastrophe occurs, entrepreneurs must know what they can expect, and the state what it must do – without months of waiting for special decisions,” states UGP, which joined the request for urgent assistance at the initiative of the association Spasimo male obiteljske iznajmljivače – SMOi (Let’s Save Small Family Landlords).

They, for their part, are demanding exemption from payment of tax and other charges at least until the end of 2026, while for 2027 they are asking that the need to continue these measures be reassessed according to the actual situation and the speed of recovery of the affected area, noting that “one cannot expect a family from whom the fire has taken the season and income to continue paying the state as if nothing had happened.”

It should also be added that the Zagreb City Administration has announced that Zagreb will donate 130 thousand euros in aid to Omiš.

World.title: Extreme Weather Inflicts Damage on Croatian Tourism and Agriculture
World.content:
August the 19th, 2026 – Extreme weather is damaging Croatian tourism and agriculture, with temperatures above 30 degrees lasting more than a month, the economic cost amounts to around one percent of GDP.

Extreme heat is becoming an increasingly significant economic risk, and Croatia could be among the more exposed European countries due to the structure of its economy. In addition to the usual summer heat, summer is the season in which temperatures are rising the fastest, the State Hydrometeorological Institute (DHMZ) revealed. Poslovni reports that from 1961 to 2020, the average summer temperature increased by between 0.3 and 0.6°C per decade, depending on the area.

In the same period, a significant increase was recorded in the number of warm days – days with a maximum daily temperature of at least 25°C – locally by up to 8.3 days per decade. “Climate change therefore does not simply mean less or more rain, but changes the timing, frequency and intensity of precipitation, and with it the associated risks,” DHMZ said. According to empirical findings for 35 countries, every additional degree above 30°C reduces labour productivity by around three percent.

risks to businesses

For companies, extreme weather conditions are no longer just a matter of meteorology or public health, but an increasingly concrete business risk. Extreme heat for some employers means fewer working hours, lower productivity, higher costs, pressure on agricultural yields and growing costs of adapting to new weather conditions. Heat thus becomes a risk that, unlike damage after a flood or storm, is often not immediately visible.

“Extreme heat creates significant business costs for European companies. According to relevant analyses, the share of lost working hours due to heat stress could rise from 1.4 percent in 1995 to 2.2–2.5 percent by 2030. According to empirical findings for 35 countries, every additional degree above 30°C reduces labour productivity by around three percent (1.3 dollars in purchasing power parity per hour of work). Among European economies, the largest drop in productivity is estimated for France, Italy and Slovenia, and Croatia does not deviate much from that trio.

In the short term, the largest part of the cost is borne by companies because wages do not decrease despite the drop in productivity, which reduces profit margins. An additional negative effect comes from warmer nights, which in 2024 caused a record 8.7 percent more lost sleep, further worsening the productivity of office workers as well,” said Hrvoje Stojić, chief economist at the Croatian Employers’ Association (HUP).

Stojić points out that in general the estimates hold that in the case of 30 or more days with temperatures above 30 degrees Celsius, the economic cost amounts to around one percent of GDP.

“What is particularly worrying is the fact that climate risks are no longer the exception, which is why they are increasingly becoming part of regular business planning. Every day of production interruption, logistics disruption or reduced employee productivity due to extreme conditions represents a direct financial cost,” said Marija Šćulac, vice-president of the Croatian Chamber of Economy (HGK). “Croatia is among the countries that are particularly exposed to climate risks, especially due to the size of its economy and the structure of the economy.

According to World Bank estimates from 2025, Croatia will need additional investments amounting to around 1.1 percent of GDP annually for successful adaptation to climate change and decarbonisation, while it is emphasised that delaying adaptation will be more expensive in the long run than timely investments. That is why we now view climate change as a matter of managing business risks,” she added. Šćulac says that the sectors most exposed to higher costs due to high temperatures are those that depend on natural conditions or are energy-intensive. Agriculture is already facing the consequences of droughts and heavy rainfall that directly reduce yields.

This is also confirmed by data from the Ministry of Agriculture. The Strategic Study for the Agriculture Strategy states that high temperatures, droughts and large amounts of precipitation negatively affect agricultural production. In addition, when maximum daily temperatures above 30°C last for more than ten consecutive days, agricultural crops enter a state of heat stress and stop growing.

In agriculture, climate risk is first seen in yields, but for Croatia its broader economic consequences could be significantly greater in tourism. According to the European Commission Report for Croatia, the direct contribution to GDP is 11.8 percent, the highest among member states, while tourism-related sectors generate around a quarter of gross value added.

risks to tourism

“Due to high temperatures, guests are changing their habits and we can expect fewer of them to come during the hottest summer months. This means that the tourism sector will have to adapt its business models to the new climate circumstances and year-round tourism. Major challenges also await the construction sector, which must find a way to organise work on construction sites during extreme heat, while logistics and transport are already feeling the consequences of disruptions caused by droughts and low water levels,” Šćulac said.

8.7 percent is what the decline in productivity stood at back in 2024 due to warmer nights. Such a development could be particularly important for Croatia, whose tourism is strongly concentrated in the summer months. The European Environment Agency warns that climate change may affect the seasonality and geographical distribution of tourist demand also because of the growing risk of extreme heat.

“Paradoxically, the sector that is key to the transition is itself highly vulnerable. The energy sector is under pressure because droughts reduce hydropower production precisely when consumption is highest. That is why it is important to develop a balanced energy mix that includes renewable sources, but also – and this is crucial – a strong and modern electricity grid that will be able to accommodate an ever-increasing number of renewable energy sources. Since extreme weather conditions affect almost all sectors, the focus is on how ready each individual sector is to manage climate risks. Companies that invest in energy efficiency, digitalisation, their own renewable energy sources and resilient infrastructure will in the long run be more competitive than those that postpone adaptation,” Šćulac said.

Examples of the impact on logistics can be found everywhere, and the Dutch one stands out in particular because the Port of Rotterdam, as the largest and one of the most important, connects maritime traffic with river, rail and road transport and enables the distribution of goods in Europe. Cargo ships transporting chemicals, oil and other goods to and from Rotterdam can, due to low water levels, be loaded only to about 30 percent of capacity in order to prevent grounding, the Financial Times reported. This means that carriers have to pay for around 100 additional river cargo ships (barges) per week, yet still cannot transport the full quantity of goods as before the drought.

The World Bank in its 2025 report for Croatia estimates that, without additional action, climate events covered by their model alone could reduce Croatian GDP by up to 2.1 percent by 2050, with infrastructure, tourism and agriculture being particularly affected.

World.title: New Croatian Toll Collection: Here’s What You Need to Know
World.content:
August the 19th, 2026 – The new Croatian motorway toll collection system will alter things as we know them quite dramatically. Here’s everything you need to know.

Poslovni reports that the new Croatian toll collection project covers the entire Croatian motorway network, including the motorways managed by Croatian Motorways, Bina Istra and the Zagreb–Macelj Motorway, meaning that Croatia should (for the first time ever) get a unified electronic toll collection system. Croatian Motorways are currently preparing one of the biggest changes in the way tolls are collected in recent decades. Classic toll booths are expected to become a thing of the past, and the new system will allow drivers to pass through motorways without stopping.

For the many drivers who already use ENC, the immediate question is: what will happen to their device? The good news is that ENC is not disappearing. On the contrary, it will remain one of the two basic methods of payment in the new system. The system will use free-flow vehicle technology, or Multi-Lane Free Flow, so it will no longer be necessary to slow down and stop in front of a barrier, tportal reports.

For passenger cars there will be two options. Drivers will be able to continue using their ENC device, while vehicles without one will be recognised by the system through automatic reading of licence plates. For heavy vehicles, ENC will be mandatory. This means that existing ENC users will not have to give up their device just because the toll booths are disappearing. What is primarily changing is the way the infrastructure will register the passage of vehicles.

The biggest change will be precisely the absence of physical barriers. Instead of approaching a barrier, slowing down and waiting, the vehicle will pass through the toll zone in the normal flow of traffic, and the system will automatically record the passage.

HAC states that tolls will continue to be calculated according to the distance travelled and the vehicle category, as is the case today. The goal of the new system is to reduce congestion, travel time, fuel consumption and emissions caused by slowing down and waiting at toll stations. The project covers the entire Croatian motorway network, including the motorways managed by Croatian Motorways, Bina Istra and the Zagreb–Macelj Motorway, so Croatia should for the first time get a unified electronic toll collection system.

An additional sign of the transition is already visible. At the beginning of July, HAC announced the gradual abolition of ARZ SMART cards, with the possibility of transferring funds to an ENC account. From the 1st of October 2026, SMART cards will no longer be usable for paying tolls. For the average driver, the most important message is therefore simple: ENC is not retiring together with the toll booths. In the new system it should become even more practical, because reading will be possible without stopping in front of a barrier.

World.title: Croatian Landlords Face Changes in Heart of Tourist Season
World.content:
August the 19th, 2026 – Croatian landlords who rent out their properties to tourists are facing changes in the very heart of the summer tourist season – and they aren’t thrilled.

We’re firmly in the middle of August, and around 250,000 guests are currently holidaying in Istria, yet even at the height of the tourist season not all accommodation capacities are full. While hotels and campsites are almost full, apartments can still be found sitting empty. Poslovni reports that this summer tourist season has so far been marked by a trend that has affected all types of accommodation – guests are increasingly waiting until the very last moment to make a reservation.

This behaviour is also changing the way Croatian landlords who do rent their properties out to tourists have to run their business this year. Lorena John, president of the Istria Family Accommodation Association, believes that the offer must adapt to guests who make their decision only a few days before travelling, HRT reports.

“Guests reserve the accommodation facility a few days before they are due to arrive. It is important that landlords adapt and count on that. I assume guests are counting on a better price, so that minimum stay is included in those discounts, that everything is regulated and that we are more flexible, and then our facilities will be full and they will prefer to stay in our property,” John said.

the price-quality ratio is more important now than ever

The large supply allows guests to wait and compare options, looking for the price-quality ratio that suits them best. Price is precisely one of the main reasons why reservations are increasingly left until the end. How much the market has changed is best illustrated by comparison with previous years. Boris Žgomba, president of the Association of Travel Agencies at the Croatian Chamber of Economy, says that the concept of last-minute now refers to a significantly larger share of capacity than before.

“Last-minute this year is completely different from what it was in previous years. In previous years last-minute was used to sell the final 20 percent of capacity a short time before arrival. However, now we have the opposite situation: 80 percent of capacity is unsold and is being sold at the last moment. And that is very, very difficult to manage,” Žgomba said. Experts point out that landlords who actively work on their offer and its improvement fare better. In such circumstances tourism can hardly be a side business, because it requires time, adaptation and continuous engagement.

travel habits are altering

How far in advance bookings are made also depends on the type of accommodation. An apartment can be filled even on the day of arrival, while for holiday homes the notion of last-minute is considerably broader. Massimo Chiavalon, owner of a travel agency, says that guest habits have also changed noticeably in that segment.

“At least 15 or 20 days in advance for us. Actually even a month is last-minute for us, because we used to be used to holiday homes being booked six months, even a year or more in advance. In the peak of the season it can still happen that guests will not find a free holiday home if they want to book at the last moment, but the last-minute booking trend is clearly visible,” Chiavalon said.

World.title: German on Croatian Tourism: “Ćevapi Aren’t Luxury Just Because They Cost 25 Euros”
World.content:
August the 18th, 2026 – A German tourist has commented on Croatian tourism and addressed the issue of prices, stating that “ćevapi don’t become a luxury dish just because they cost 25 euros”.

A German who has been coming to the central Dalmatian island of Brač for 18 years, bought a house and fully integrated into the local community, has sent an open letter about the changes in Croatian tourism. The website Kroatien-nachrichten.de published a letter from “a long-time German visitor that every restaurateur and mayor should read.” Poslovni reports that Christoph, the aforementioned German entrepreneur from Frankfurt, sent an emotional and insightful open letter in which he warns about worrying trends in Croatian tourism.

His words aren’t the reaction of a dissatisfied tourist who is just passing through, but the deep reflection of a man who considers the island his second home. Consequently, he witnesses first-hand how the pursuit of profit and commercialisation is gradually undermining the very foundations of the Dalmatian way of life. Reflecting on the change in the local mentality and everyday life, Christoph recalls the time when the tourist season was only a part of life, not the sole reason for existence.

“things cost as much as they do in frankfurt”

“We got to know Croatia as a warm, open and hospitable country. Even in the middle of the season, our friends here had time for coffee, conversation, a shared dinner or spontaneous gatherings… People had to earn a living then, just as they do now. But the season was part of their lives; it was not their whole life,” the author emphasises, adding that the logic of business and pricing in hospitality has fundamentally changed since then.

Comparing the costs with those in his hometown, he notes that “simple ćevapčići or a pljeskavica cost 20 or 25 euros, while a steak costs 35 euros,” highlighting the absurdity of the situation:

“I come from Frankfurt. We are also familiar with high prices there… But when a simple meal on Brač costs as much as a meal in the centre of Frankfurt, it is hard for me – as an entrepreneur – to justify it economically.” What is particularly worrying is that the focus has shifted from a fair price for the service to how much more can be extracted from the guest. The author explains that the reluctance of long-time guests to spend is not the result of a lack of funds, but a loss of perspective regarding true value. “Sometimes it seems as if the question is: How much more can the guest pay? How high can I raise the price before they say: ‘Enough!’? … The problem is not that we cannot afford it. We could. But we are less and less willing to pay, because we no longer feel that the price corresponds to what we get in return.”

“everything has a price”

This relentless commercialisation is visible even in the smallest details of the environment – such as showers in public spaces.

“For years there was a simple shower in our public cove that the municipality had installed. You would come out of the sea, rinse off the salt and go home. No one thought about it. Today there is a coin-operated shower. Of course, no one will go bankrupt paying one euro for a shower. It’s not about the euro itself; it’s about whether everything has to have a price,” says Christoph.

In addition to the financial pressure, what personally affects the author the most is the administrative distancing and the loss of the local connection with the vessel – despite decades of investment and participation in the local community. Consequently, a sense of alienation reappears. Regarding his reaction to the news that he is no longer considered a resident, he writes: “The message we receive is: You don’t really belong here. And that hurts… Through friendships, neighbourhood, trust and returning year after year… After so many years we no longer felt like tourists. And yet, today we increasingly feel that we are only guests – guests from whom a lot of money is expected to be spent.” In conclusion, the author appeals to local business owners and decision-makers not to sacrifice authenticity and long-term relationships for short-term profit. He reminds them that Croatia has no need to imitate other mass markets or exclusive tourist destinations, because its charm lies in its simplicity and its people.

“Croatia was never the Côte d’Azur for us, and that’s a compliment”

“For us, Croatia was never the Côte d’Azur. And I mean that as a compliment to Croatia. We weren’t looking for Saint-Tropez. We were looking for Brač… Ćevapčići do not become a luxury dish just because they cost 25 euros. A konoba does not become a luxury restaurant just because dinner costs 100 euros per person,” Christoph concludes with a final message about the value of hard-earned trust: “Prices can be changed again. Houses can be renovated. Roads can be repaired. But trust, the feeling of welcome and the sense of belonging are much harder to regain once they are lost. Hold on to that. It is worth more than earning another euro.”

World.title: Higher Price Growth in Greece, Spain and Cyprus Than Croatia
World.content:
August the 18th, 2026 – Despite the focus constantly being on this country, it seems that there’s been higher price growth in Greece, Spain and Cyprus than in Croatia.

As Jadranka Dozan reports for Poslovni, Croatian prices in tourism had risen to 95 percent of the EU average by 2024, but last year they grew faster in the rest of the EU. That brought Croatia back below 90 percent of the average. This means that Croatia currently remains among the more expensive destinations in the Mediterranean, but the direction of price competitiveness is also important to note.

Growth rates in hospitality and accommodation signal that our price competitiveness is roughly the same as last year. State statisticians confirmed the preliminary estimate of July inflation from two weeks ago: prices of goods and services for household personal consumption fell for the third month in a row on a monthly basis (by 0.2 percent in July) and slowed their annual growth. The annual rate was reduced to 3.9 percent, and this slowdown is the result of current pressures and base effects that are particularly pronounced in food prices (the increase in July last year). According to the harmonised index (HICP), which also includes the consumption of foreign tourists and is used as a measure of inflation in comparisons with other EU members, the annual price growth slowed from 4.2 to 3.6 percent.

Besides the fact that we are no longer at or near the very top of the Eurozone ranking, inflation in the rest of the zone accelerated slightly in July (from 2.8 to 2.9 percent), so the inflation gap has also narrowed; Croatia is now “only” 0.7 percentage points above the average.

price policies and adjustments

From the 1st of July to the 13th of August, hospitality turnover stood at around 1.32 billion euros, or 10.8 percent higher than last year, with 6.8 percent more invoices issued. Among the main groups of goods and services according to the CBS categorisation, seasonal discounts on clothing and footwear contributed most to the July monthly decline (prices fell 13%). The largest monthly increase is also seasonal in nature: in Restaurants and accommodation services, prices rose by an average of 3.4 percent in July after June’s +2.2 percent. On an annual basis they also accelerated growth, from 5.8 to 6.3 percent, but this is still lower than for total services, which are currently at +8.5 percent.

It is also worth noting that the average annual growth in prices in hospitality and accommodation in the first seven months was 6.2 percent compared with 8.9 percent in the same period last year. Moreover, compared with tourist competitors from the south of the EU, the annual growth of these prices in Croatia in the middle of the year (according to HICP, 4.9 percent) was lower than in, for example, Greece, Cyprus and Spain (8.9, 6.4 and 5.3 percent respectively). This could also be a signal that in terms of tourism price competitiveness, Croatia remains more or less holding last year’s positions relative to our main competitors.

After the price level of these services in Croatia rose from 84 to 95 percent of the EU average between 2022 and 2024, in the rest of the Union they grew faster in 2025, which brought us back below 90 percent (to 89.6) of the average of all member states. While all of the above does mean that Croatia remains among the more expensive destinations in the Mediterranean, the direction of price competitiveness is significant, as touched on previously.

higher turnover

At the peak of the 2026 summer tourist season, fiscalisation data suggests some very solid indicators of turnover in final consumption. From the beginning of July to the 13th of August in cafes, restaurants and other forms of food and drink preparation and service across Croatia, 6.8 percent more receipts and invoices were issued than last year, while the 1.32 billion euros of recorded turnover means a nominal increase of 10.8 percent.

In the provision of accommodation in those just under a month and a half, 1.11 billion euros passed through fiscal cash registers, or 14.8 percent more turnover than last year, with 6.2 percent more invoices. The difference in percentage growth is partly attributed to price increases, but may also reflect a higher average number of overnight stays per invoice. At the same time, retail trade turnover in Croatia from the beginning of July to 13 August exceeded 4.43 billion, which is a year-on-year increase of seven percent, achieved on 3.1 percent more invoices issued.

The significantly smaller percentage difference between the number of invoices and turnover in retail reflects the slower growth in the prices of goods, including those that make up a significant part of tourist consumption. This is particularly true for supermarkets and hypermarkets or so-called non-specialised stores predominantly selling food, drink and tobacco. Thus, for example, prices of Food and non-alcoholic beverages after a slight June decline rose very little in July (by 0.4 percent), but in the annual comparison, after a slowdown in growth (to 1.4% in May and 0.8% in June), in July they were on average at approximately the same level as a year earlier or a symbolic 0.1 percent lower than in July 2025.

World.title: Iran’s Ghalibaf in Iraq to push regional cooperation
World.content:
Baghdad — Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Wednesday stressed the importance of strengthening the “new order” in the region, on the first stop in a three-day visit to Iraq.

Ghalibaf’s trip comes at a time when Iraq is facing American pressure to disarm factions close to Tehran, which wields significant political influence in Iraq.

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who took office three months ago with US backing, has pledged to restrict weapons to the control of the state.

Speaking from the site near Baghdad airport where Iranian general Qassem Soleimani was killed in a 2020 US strike, Ghalibaf said: “Our trip to Iraq today is aimed at strengthening the new order in the region and accelerating the strengthening of cooperation between all countries in the region without foreign interference.”

“Resistance in Iraq is… one of the elements of this country’s power. Today, resistance has gone beyond the borders of Iran and Iraq… and has become global,” he added.

Ghalibaf is scheduled to meet Zaidi later on Wednesday and then hold a meeting with the Coordination Framework, the largest bloc in parliament, made up of Shia parties with varying degrees of proximity to Tehran.

Iraq has been pulled into the Middle East war, with pro-Iran factions have launching attacks on US interests, which Washington has responded to with deadly strikes. Iran has also shelled positions belonging to Iranian Kurdish opposition groups.

Iraq is facing mounting challenges in maintaining a balance between Iran and the United States, and since the US invasion in 2003 it has been an arena of rivalry between the two powers.

Zaidi has given the armed factions — some of which belong to the Iran-backed Axis of Resistance — until September 30 to hand over their weapons to the state, coinciding with the scheduled end of the mission of the US-led coalition against the Islamic State group.

Some of the most powerful factions, however, and those closest to Iran, refuse to cooperate.

On Thursday, Ghalibaf will head to the holy city of Karbala where he will take part in ceremonies marking 40 days since the funeral of former Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei, who was killed in US-Israeli strikes on February 28.

World.title: Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council president arrives in Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The President of Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council, Faiq Zaidan, and the Saudi Justice Minister, Walid al-Samaani, discussed on Wednesday approaches to enhance judicial and legal cooperation between Iraq and Saudi Arabia.

During their meeting in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, the two sides discussed ways to deepen judicial and legal relations by enhancing cooperation between the institutions of the two countries.

Zaidan, accompanied by a high-level Iraqi judicial delegation, arrived on Wednesday morning in Riyadh in response to the Saudi Minister of Justice’s official invitation.

The Iraqi delegation includes the chief prosecutor, the Head of the Judicial Oversight Authority, and the Director of the General Department of Judicial Guards.

The visit is part of a larger effort to deepen judicial and legal relations between Iraq and Saudi Arabia, as well as to develop areas of cooperation between the two countries’ relevant institutions.

Iraq and Saudi Arabia are eagerly enhancing bilateral legal and judicial cooperation through high-level diplomatic visits, institutional coordination, and joint executive training programs to share experience and strengthen cross-border stability.

Zidan had previously attended formal consultations in Riyadh with Saudi judiciary authorities to improve institutional communication and evaluate mutual security-related court files.

Ongoing coordination supports broader dialogue between Iraqi judicial bodies and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) authorities to address regional legal and security issues.

World.title: Israel army admits firing on car in death of five-year-old Hind Rajab
World.content:
Jerusalem – The Israeli military on Wednesday admitted its troops fired on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing which drew international outrage.

Hind Rajab’s body was recovered from a car riddled with bullets in Gaza City days after she was last heard from in a desperate, hours-long phone call to the Palestinian Red Crescent on January 29, 2024.

The Israeli military had previously denied its troops were present in the area near the incident.

“Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by Military Police Criminal Investigation Division,” the military said on Wednesday.

The military also published reviews into four other high-profile incidents in Gaza, saying it was launching a criminal probe into the 2025 killing of 15 Palestinian medics and humanitarian personnel.

Hind Rajab had made the emergency call after her family’s car came under fire during an attempt to flee Gaza City amid an Israeli advance.

Her body was eventually recovered along with those of six relatives and two Red Crescent rescuers sent to find her.

Her death sparked international outrage and calls for an independent investigation, and the original audio recordings of her emergency call were incorporated into the Oscar-nominated feature film “The Voice of Hind Rajab”.

The Israeli military said on Wednesday its findings indicated troops had “fired at a vehicle that was approaching them while travelling contrary to the advance notice” that had been given to residents in the area.

It said the initial fire killed five of the passengers, while Hind Rajab and her cousin Layan Hamada survived.

The military said movement of a Palestine Red Crescent ambulance had then been coordinated in order to evacuate the casualties.

“However, according to the allegations raised, upon the ambulance’s arrival at the scene of the incident, a shell was fired toward it, resulting in the deaths of the two paramedics travelling in it,” it added.

The Hind Rajab Foundation, a Brussels-based legal organisation seeking to address alleged Israeli violations in Gaza, said it had “no confidence” in the Israeli military probe.

“These reported investigations, even if they do occur, should not be mistaken for a genuine step toward justice,” it said in a statement.

– ‘Deeply offensive’ –

The military said criminal investigations would not be launched into three other incidents, involving the killing of seven employees from World Central Kitchen and four from Doctors Without Borders (MSF), both of which drew international scrutiny.

The founder of World Central Kitchen, Jose Andres, said on X that the decision was “wrong and is painful for all of us. There was no excuse for their attacks on our team.”

The US-based charity called the decision “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”, demanding “an independent commission to investigate the airstrikes because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct”.

The military said it had ordered a criminal probe into the killing of 15 Palestinian medics and humanitarian personnel in southern Gaza in March 2025, in another incident that sparked widespread outrage.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said at the time that a team of first responders was killed by Israeli forces on March 23, 2025 and that other emergency and aid teams were hit one after another over several hours while searching for their missing colleagues.

Those killed included eight Red Crescent staff, six members of the Gaza civil defence agency and one employee of the UN agency for Palestinian refugees.

The bodies were found buried near Gaza’s southernmost city of Rafah in what OCHA described as a mass grave.

The military said three shooting incidents occurred on that day, with fire directed at rescue vehicles including a fire truck, ambulances and a UN vehicle during an ambush against Hamas operatives.

It said 15 Palestinians were killed including medics, claiming “six of those killed were identified as belonging to Hamas”.

Troops then decided to “crush the vehicles and to cover the bodies with metal mesh”, it said.

“Having found that the firing conducted during the incident raises a reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident,” it added.

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Turk, said at the time that the incident raised “further concerns over the commission of war crimes by the Israeli military”.

World.title: Germany, France, UN condemn far-right Israeli minister’s ‘inhumane’ Gaza remarks
World.content:
Berlin – Germany, France and the UN on Wednesday condemned remarks by Israel’s far-right national security minister, who declared that Israel should kill “30 or 40” people every night in the Palestinian territory of Gaza.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz “strongly condemns the inhumane appeals made by Minister (Itamar) Ben Gvir, which violate international law,” German government spokesman Sebastian Hille said. “They are unacceptable.”

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also slammed the remarks, calling them “intolerable and inhumane” in an interview with the La Montagne regional newspaper.

United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres described them as “appalling. They’re outrageous. They’re dehumanizing, and they’re dangerous,” his spokesman said.

Israel launched a military campaign on Hamas-ruled Gaza after the October 7, 2023 attack by Palestinian militant group Hamas.

Ben Gvir, who is already facing calls from several European countries for bloc-wide sanctions, made the call for mass killings during a podcast with a former Gaza hostage who had been held by Hamas.

“I think targeted eliminations should be carried out in Gaza every night. Take out 30 or 40,” he said.

“Not only those who endanger you right now. These are people who shouldn’t be alive,” Ben Gvir said. “I’m paying them a compliment by calling them humans.”

Lars Klingbeil, German vice chancellor and finance minister, said in a TV interview Tuesday that Ben Gvir’s comments “must have consequences”, adding that sanctions were being discussed at the European level.

Several European countries have called for EU-wide sanctions against the far-right minister, but the proposal has failed to win the required unanimity.

Calls to blacklist Ben Gvir grew after he published a video in May of himself mocking bound activists seized by Israeli soldiers on a Gaza-bound aid flotilla.

France in response banned Ben Gvir from entering the country and called for the EU to impose bloc-wide sanctions.

But EU sanctions have to be signed off by all 27 member states and staunch supporters of Israel refused to go along with the push.

– ‘No further steps’ –

Germany also condemned Israeli plans for settlement expansion in the so-called E1 area of the occupied West Bank, saying it jeopardises the prospect for a two-state solution.

“Our message is clear: there must be no further steps toward annexation in the West Bank,” said Hille.

“No formal ones, but also no political, structural, or other measures whose impact is increasingly and obviously leading toward annexation. They run counter to a two-state solution.”

France’s Barrot did not rule out further sanctions on Israeli settlers in the West Bank, who have increasingly been harassing and assaulting Palestinian residents in recent months, often with the aim to take their property.

“We imposed European sanctions against these settlers for the third time on May 28,” he said.

“Further sanctions could be imposed and all options are on the table,” Barrot added.

Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967 and successive Israeli governments have expanded settlements.

But they have accelerated significantly under the current coalition government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Excluding east Jerusalem, more than 500,000 Israelis now live in the West Bank in settlements that are illegal under international law, among some three million Palestinians.

World.title: Golden Shoe winner Kane hopes for Ballon d’Or after ‘best season ever’
World.content:
Munich – Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has set his sights on the Ballon d’Or after receiving his second European Golden Shoe in Munich on Wednesday.

The England captain collected the prize after scoring the most goals in Europe’s top divisions last season.

Kane won the 2023-24 award after a prolific first season at Bayern, but said this year’s honour “tasted even better than the first”.

The 33-year-old scored 36 goals in 31 Bundesliga games last term, the third most in a German top-flight campaign, while winning the league and cup double.

He also netted six times at the World Cup, becoming England’s top goalscorer at the competition with 14 career goals.

In total, he scored 73 goals for club and country last season.

Kane said he hoped to receive football’s highest individual honour after his “best season ever”.

“Obviously, that’s out of my control. I know, of course, there’s going to be a lot of talk about it from now until October when it’s announced,” he said.

“Ultimately, I’ve done everything I can last season. It was my best season by far. I achieved a lot with the teams I was in.”

Kane made it to the Champions League semi-finals with Bayern, who were narrowly defeated by eventual winners Paris Saint-Germain.

He also reached the semi-finals of the World Cup with England before an agonising 2-1 loss to Argentina.

Only serial Ballon d’Or winners Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo have won the Golden Shoe more often than Kane.

Messi won the award six times, all with Barcelona, while Ronaldo won it three times at Real Madrid and once at Manchester United.

“That’s for you guys to debate and fans to debate,” Kane said of the possible winner of this year’s Ballon d’Or, which will be handed out in London in late October.

“That’s what makes the Ballon d’Or so special as well. Many players have had great seasons.”

Kane said on Monday he was about to begin negotiations to extend his contract at Bayern, which will expire in 2027.

World.title: Iraq in negotiations with German firm to secure safe passage via Hormuz
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) is in serious discussions with a German shipping firm to secure safe passage for crude oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz on Iraqi-flagged tankers, leveraging an initial arrangement with Iran to avoid regional shipping restrictions in the waterway.

According to local news outlet Shafaq News, Baghdad requires all chartered transit vessels to fly the Iraqi flag.

While an American firm rejected this term, the German shipping company accepted the condition to transport crude from Iraq’s southern ports.

Tehran has agreed in principle to waive transit costs for Iraqi-flagged vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

Haibat al-Halbousi, Iraq’s parliament speaker, met with Iranian authorities to request special treatment to protect Iraq’s economic interests.

Iraq still requires explicit US authority or sanctions clearance to complete the agreement. The step is necessary due to the United States’ stringent restrictions on shipping, insurance, and transit systems associated with Iranian territorial waters.

This agreement is part of a bigger drive by Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s cabinet, which recently approved an emergency three-month mechanism to diversify export routes through specialized local and foreign enterprises beginning September 1.

The Iraqi government approved oil purchases at a lower price compared to the official rate of SOMO with an annual 30 percent discount.

World.title: Terrorists killed in airstrikes in northern Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Security Media Cell (ISMC) confirmed on Monday that airstrikes successfully eliminated a group of terrorists in the Zaghitoun Valley area in the northern Iraqi province of Kirkuk.

After receiving comprehensive information from the Military Intelligence Directorate, Iraqi security forces discovered an active terrorist hideaway, according to a statement cited by the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).

F-16 fighter jets of the Iraqi Air Force launched two successive attacks, destroying and killing all terrorists sheltering within the hideout.

The statement did not indicate the number of casualties or disclose their identities, nor did it provide further details regarding the nature of the targeted group.

The ISMC affirmed that the Iraqi armed forces are continuing to pursue terrorist hideouts throughout the country.

The operation is part of ongoing security efforts aimed at targeting ISIS terrorists in the Zaghitoun Valley, an area that has recently experienced multiple Iraqi ground operations and airstrikes.

On July 20, the Joint Operations Command announced the destruction of six ISIS hideouts in the Zaghitoun Valley as part of an intelligence-driven security operation that included area sweeps.

On May 23, Iraqi F-16 fighter jets also carried out an airstrike targeting an ISIS position in the same area.

World.title: Iraq, Saudi Arabia discuss regional developments
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein and his Saudi counterpart, Faisal bin Farhan, discussed on Tuesday regional developments and approaches to de-escalate tensions.

The two ministers stressed the need to de-escalate the situation and return to dialogue, according to a statement cited by the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).

During their phone conversation, the two sides discussed developments in the region in light of growing tensions and the significant implications for regional security and stability.

Hussein and Fuad discussed measures for resolving issues peacefully, preventing tensions from rising and ensuring regional stability.

Hussein stated that continuing collaboration between the two nations, as well as with other countries in the region, is critical to settling the ongoing conflict.

The coordination between Baghdad and Riyadh follows US-Saudi attacks on Iran-linked militia locations in several Iraqi provinces on July 29.

Baghdad’s security cooperation with Riyadh has grown more vital as the government seeks to prevent Iran-backed militias from drawing Iraq into a larger regional conflict.

World.content:
The 20-member panel includes faculty members from JNU, Delhi University, Ignou, National Law University Delhi, Jindal Global Law School, Pondicherry University and Utkal University.

NEW DELHI: NCERT has reconstituted the team tasked with preparing political science textbooks for Classes XI and XII, bringing together university academics, schoolteachers and its own faculty members, with the first of the two books scheduled to be ready by Nov.The 20-member panel includes faculty members from JNU, Delhi University, Ignou, National Law University Delhi, Jindal Global Law School, Pondicherry University and Utkal University, schoolteachers and NCERT academics, with at least four of its members known for links, past or present, with organisations linked to RSS or BJP.They are former ABVP national secretary and JNU professor Vandana Mishra; educationist Yadunath Deshpande, who has held organisational positions in ABVP and has described himself professionally as a BJP political consultant; Prashant Divekar of Pune-based Jnana Prabodhini; and JNU academic Ravi Rameshchandra Shukla, who has been associated with the editorial board of a journal published by Rambhau Mhalgi Prabodhini-linked Indian Institute of Democratic Leadership.The composition of the panel, however, is considerably broader, with it also having Prakash Kandpal and Ravi Shukla from JNU, Needhi Gupta from NLU Delhi, Chetan Singhai from Chanakya University, Sukanshika Vatsa from Delhi University and Satish Kumar from Ignou, among others.The Textbook Development Team (TDT), headed by political analyst and academic Sandeep Shastri, vice-president of Nitte (Deemed to be University), has been asked to finalise the Class XI textbook by Nov 30, 2026, and the Class XII book by July 30, 2027.NCERT said the reconstitution of the team was intended to "further strengthen and streamline" preparation of the two textbooks. The final teaching-learning material will be approved, published and distributed by NCERT.According to NCERT's Aug 14 notification, the team will work under National Curriculum Framework for School Education, 2023, and seek guidance from curricular groups dealing with social science, languages, Indian Knowledge Systems, environmental education and pedagogy. The books will also be reviewed for themes that include cultural rootedness, inclusion, educational technology, assessment and Indian Knowledge Systems.

World.title: Sunali Khatun's husband joins her, SC closes case
World.content: NEW DELHI: Six months after bringing back a pregnant Sunali Khatun and her son from Bangladesh on orders of SC, her father's counsel Wednesday informed the court that her husband has also been repatriated to India and joined the family in Bengal.Sunali and her family were picked up from Delhi during an identification verification drive on June 24 last year and all members of them were pushed into Bangladesh from Assam on June 26.Sunali's father Bhodu Sekh had moved Calcutta HC, which had termed the deportations illegal and directed govt to bring them back Govt appealed against the HC order before SC, on whose directions Sunali and her son were brought back on Dec 5, 2025. tnn

World.title: Paternity test of child can be allowed in marital dispute: SC
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Though the legitimacy of a child born during marriage is presumed,

Wednesday held that a child can be subjected to a paternity test in a matrimonial dispute in which a man has sought divorce on the ground of alleged unchaste character of his wife and has claimed that he is not the child's biological father.

A bench of Justices M M Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale rejected the plea of a woman who had opposed a paternity test of the child. She contended it was a settled principle of law that no party can be forced to undergo a DNA test, and the divorce plea of her husband should be decided without the paternity test.

"If you are loyal, then why should you object to the test," the bench asked. It upheld orders passed by a family court in Pune and Bombay HC directing a DNA test in divorce proceedings initiated by the husband, who submitted that the allegation of unchastity could be proved only through a DNA test.

In this case, the husband had privately undergone a DNA test, which returned a negative result, thus showing that he was not the biological father of the child. Armed with the report, he filed a divorce petition and sought a court-directed DNA test to prove his allegations.

"In the facts of the present case, to prove the prima facie case, the husband has placed on record DNA test carried out by the laboratory at Hyderabad which concludes that the probability of him being the father...





is zero. Such DNA report obtained by the petitioner would form prima facie and sufficient material to conclude that the direction for undergoing DNA test can be issued. The second parameter is eminent need.

The averments in the petition indicate that unchastity of the petitioner is the main ground pleaded by husband for getting divorce. A DNA test report would be of material bearing to prove the fact whether he is the father of son named in the petition.

Considering the allegations made in the petition, it would be difficult to get conclusive evidence to prove such allegation, except the DNA report," the HC had said in its order.

The apex court upheld the HC order, paving the way for a paternity test of the child.

"The petition is based on the allegations of unchastity made against the wife. Result of DNA test would establish the allegations in the petition. Therefore, in my opinion, the husband satisfied the parameter of eminent need required to be taken into consideration by the Court while passing order of undergoing DNA test," the high court had said.

World.title: UP gets Japan investment boost with projects worth Rs 3000 crore
World.content:
NEW DELHI/LUCKNOW: CM Yogi Adityanath Wednesday invited Japanese companies to make UP their "second home" as the state received a major investment boost with the virtual groundbreaking of two Japan-backed projects worth Rs 3,191 crore in the Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority region.

Addressing the inaugural session of UP-Japan Investment Meet 2026 in New Delhi, Yogi pitched the state as a long-term industrial partner for Japan, calling for cooperation not only in manufacturing but also in technology, research and development, skill development and global supply chains. "We want them to consider UP their second industrial home," the CM said.

The projects are the outcome of investment outreach, with the CM visiting Japan in Feb and inviting companies there to invest in UP.
